In [[mathematics]], '''Johnson graphs''' are a special class of [[undirected graph]]s defined from systems of sets. The vertices of the Johnson graph <math>J(n,k)</math> are the <math>k</math>-element [[subset]]s of an <math>n</math>-element set; two vertices are adjacent when the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the two vertices (subsets) contains <math>(k-1)</math>-elements.<ref name="hs93">{{citation
 | last1 = Holton | first1 = D. A.
 | last2 = Sheehan | first2 = J.
 | contribution = The Johnson graphs and even graphs
 | doi = 10.1017/CBO9780511662058
 | isbn = 0-521-43594-3
 | location = Cambridge
 | mr = 1232658
 | page = 300
 | publisher = Cambridge University Press
 | series = Australian Mathematical Society Lecture Series
 | title = The Petersen graph
 | title-link = The Petersen Graph
 | contribution-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=sMSOSgbCx3kC&pg=PA300
 | volume = 7
 | year = 1993}}.</ref> Both Johnson graphs and the closely related [[Johnson scheme]] are named after [[Selmer M. Johnson]].

==Special cases==
*Both <math>J(n,1)</math> and <math>J(n,n-1)</math> are the [[complete graph]] {{mvar|K<sub>n</sub>}}.
*<math>J(4,2)</math> is the [[octahedral graph]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Stanić | first = Zoran
 | year = 2017
 | title = Regular Graphs: A Spectral Approach
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=igLEDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA63
 | page = 63&ndash;64
 | publisher = de Gruyter
 | isbn = 978-3-11-035135-4
}}</ref>
*<math>J(5,2)</math> is the [[complement graph|complement]] of the [[Petersen graph]],<ref name="hs93"/> hence the [[line graph]] of {{math|''K''<sub>5</sub>}}. More generally, for all <math>n</math>, the Johnson graph <math>J(n,2)</math> is the line graph of {{mvar|K<sub>n</sub>}} and the complement of the [[Kneser graph]] <math>K(n,2).</math>

==Graph-theoretic properties==
* <math>J(n,k)</math> is [[graph isomorphism|isomorphic]] to <math>J(n,n-k).</math>
* For all <math>0 \leq j \leq \operatorname{diam}(J(n,k))</math>, any pair of vertices at distance <math>j</math> share <math>k-j</math> elements in common.
* <math>J(n,k)</math> is [[Hamilton-connected]], meaning that every pair of vertices forms the endpoints of a [[Hamiltonian path]] in the graph. In particular this means that it has a [[Hamiltonian cycle]].<ref>{{citation|last=Alspach|first=Brian|title=Johnson graphs are Hamilton-connected| year=2013| authorlink=Brian Alspach|journal=Ars Mathematica Contemporanea|volume=6|issue=1|pages=21–23|doi=10.26493/1855-3974.291.574|doi-access=free}}.</ref>
* It is also known that the Johnson graph <math>J(n,k)</math> is <math>k(n-k)</math>-vertex-connected.<ref>{{citation|title=On Connectivity of the Facet Graphs of Simplicial Complexes|year=2015|last1=Newman|last2=Rabinovich|first1=Ilan|first2=Yuri|arxiv=1502.02232|bibcode=2015arXiv150202232N}}.</ref> 
* <math>J(n,k)</math> forms the [[Graph of a polytope|vertex-edge graph]] of an (''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)-dimensional [[polytope]], called a [[hypersimplex]].<ref>{{citation|last=Rispoli|first=Fred J.|title=The graph of the hypersimplex|year=2008|arxiv=0811.2981|bibcode=2008arXiv0811.2981R}}.</ref> 
* Any [[maximal clique]] is either of the form <math>\{ S \cup \{x \} \mid x \in \{1, \dots, n\}  \setminus S \}</math> for a <math>(k - 1)</math>-element subset <math>S</math> and <math>k < n - 1</math>, or of the form <math>\{S \setminus \{x\} \mid x \in S\}</math> for a <math>(k + 1)</math>-element set <math>S</math> for <math>k > 1</math>, or of the form <math>\{\{1\}, \{2\}\}</math> in the edge case <math>(n, k) = (2, 1)</math>.<ref>{{citation|title=The automorphism group of a Johnson graph|last1=Ramras|last2=Donovan|first1=Mark|first2=Elizabeth|year=2011|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|volume=25|issue=1|pages=267–270|doi=10.1137/090765596}}</ref>
* The [[clique number]] of <math>J(n,k)</math> is given by an expression in terms of its least and greatest [[eigenvalue]]s: <math>\omega(J(n,k)) = 1 - \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}</math>, or, by the above explicit description of maximal cliques, <math>\omega(J(n,k)) = \max\{k + 1, n - k + 1\}.</math>
* The [[clique cover number]] of <math>J(n, k)</math> satisfies <math>\theta(J(n, 1)) = 1</math> for <math>n > 1</math>, <math>\theta(J(n, 2)) = n - 2</math> for <math>n > 2</math> and <math>\theta(J(n, 3)) = \lfloor (n-1)^2/4 \rfloor</math> for <math>n > 5</math> but is not known in general.<ref>{{citation|title=On the clique covering numbers of Johnson graphs|last=Jørgensen|first=Søren F.|year=2025|journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography|volume=93|issue=9|pages=3689–3705|doi=10.1007/s10623-025-01663-3|arxiv=2502.15019}}</ref>
* The [[chromatic number]] of <math>J(n,k)</math> is at most <math>n, \chi(J(n,k)) \leq n.</math><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.win.tue.nl/~aeb/graphs/Johnson.html|title=Johnson|website=www.win.tue.nl|access-date=2017-07-26}}</ref>
* Each Johnson graph is ''locally grid'', meaning that the [[induced subgraph]] of the [[Neighbourhood (graph theory)|neighbors]] of any vertex is a [[rook's graph]]. More precisely, in the Johnson graph <math>J(n,k)</math>, each neighborhood is a <math>k\times (n-k)</math> rook's graph.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Cohen | first = Arjeh M.
 | editor1-last = Kantor | editor1-first = William M.
 | editor2-last = Liebler | editor2-first = Robert A.
 | editor3-last = Payne | editor3-first = Stanley E.
 | editor4-last = Shult | editor4-first = Ernest E.
 | contribution = Local recognition of graphs, buildings, and related geometries
 | contribution-url = https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1882013/588207.pdf
 | mr = 1072157
 | pages = 85–94
 | publisher = Oxford University Press
 | series = Oxford Science Publications
 | title = Finite Geometries, Buildings, and Related Topics: Papers from the Conference on Buildings and Related Geometries held in Pingree Park, Colorado, July 17–23, 1988
 | year = 1990}}; see in particular pp. 89–90</ref>

== Automorphism group ==
There is a [[distance-transitive graph|distance-transitive]] [[subgroup]] of <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J(n,k))</math> [[group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to <math>\operatorname{Sym}(n)</math>. In fact, <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J(n,k)) \cong \operatorname{Sym}(n)</math>, except that when <math>n = 2k \geq 4</math>, <math>\operatorname{Aut}(J(n,k)) \cong \operatorname{Sym}(n) \times C_2</math>.<ref name=":0">{{citation|title=Distance-Regular Graphs|last=Brouwer |first=Andries E.|date=1989|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|others=Cohen, Arjeh M., Neumaier, Arnold.|isbn=9783642743436|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|oclc=851840609}}</ref>

== Intersection array ==
As a consequence of being distance-transitive, <math>J(n,k)</math> is also [[distance-regular graph|distance-regular]]. Letting <math>d</math> denote its [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]], the intersection array of <math>J(n,k)</math> is given by 

:<math>\left\{ b_{0}, \ldots, b_{d-1}, c_{1}, \ldots c_{d} \right \}</math> 

where:

:<math>\begin{align}
b_{j} &= (k - j)(n - k - j)  && 0 \leq j < d \\
c_{j} &= j^2  && 0 < j \leq d 
\end{align}</math>

It turns out that unless <math>J(n,k)</math> is <math>J(8,2)</math>, its intersection array is not shared with any other distinct distance-regular graph; the intersection array of <math>J(8,2)</math> is shared with three other distance-regular graphs that are not Johnson graphs.<ref name="hs93" />

== Eigenvalues and eigenvectors ==
* The characteristic polynomial of <math>J(n,k)</math> is given by 
::<math>\phi(x) := \prod_{j=0}^{\operatorname{diam}(J(n,k))} \left (x-A_{n,k}(j)\right )^{\binom{n}{j} - \binom{n}{j-1}}.</math>
:where <math>A_{n,k}(j) = (k-j)(n-k-j)-j.</math><ref name=":0" />

* The [[eigenvector]]s of <math>J(n,k)</math> have an explicit description.<ref>{{citation|last=Filmus|first=Yuval|title=An Orthogonal Basis for Functions over a Slice of the Boolean Hypercube|journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics |year=2014|volume=23 |article-number=P1.23 |doi=10.37236/4567 |arxiv=1406.0142|bibcode=2014arXiv1406.0142F|s2cid=7416206 }}.</ref>

==Johnson scheme==
The Johnson graph <math>J(n,k)</math> is closely related to the [[Johnson scheme]], an [[association scheme]] in which each pair of {{mvar|k}}-element sets is associated with a number, half the size of the [[symmetric difference]] of the two sets.<ref name="c99">{{citation|last=Cameron|first=Peter J.|title=Permutation Groups|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4bNj8K1omGAC&pg=PA95|year=1999|series=London Mathematical Society Student Texts|volume=45|page=95|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780521653787}}.</ref> The Johnson graph has an edge for every pair of sets at distance one in the association scheme, and the distances in the association scheme are exactly the [[shortest path]] distances in the Johnson graph.<ref>The explicit identification of graphs with association schemes, in this way, can be seen in {{citation | last = Bose | first = R. C.
 | journal = Pacific Journal of Mathematics | mr = 0157909 | pages = 389–419 | title = Strongly regular graphs, partial geometries and partially balanced designs | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | year = 1963 | doi=10.2140/pjm.1963.13.389| doi-access = free }}.</ref>

The Johnson scheme is also related to another family of distance-transitive graphs, the [[odd graph]]s, whose vertices are <math>k</math>-element subsets of an <math>(2k+1)</math>-element set and whose edges correspond to [[disjoint sets|disjoint]] pairs of subsets.<ref name="c99"/>

== Open problems ==
The vertex-expansion properties of Johnson graphs, as well as the structure of the corresponding extremal sets of vertices of a given size, are not fully understood. However, an asymptotically tight lower bound on expansion of large sets of vertices was recently obtained.<ref>{{citation|title=An Approximate Vertex-Isoperimetric Inequality for $r$-sets |year=2013 |last1=Christofides |last2=Ellis |last3=Keevash |first1=Demetres |first2=David |first3=Peter|journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics|volume=4|issue=20}}.</ref>

In general, determining the chromatic number of a Johnson graph is an [[open problem]].<ref>{{citation|title=Erdős-Ko-Rado theorems : algebraic approaches|last1=Godsil |first1=C. D.|last2=Meagher |first2=Karen |isbn=9781107128446|location=Cambridge, United Kingdom|publisher=Cambridge University Press|oclc=935456305|year = 2016}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=On the chromatic number of Grassmann graphs|last1=D'haeseleer |first1=Jozefien|last2=Taranchuk|first2=Vladislav|journal=Linear Algebra and its Applications|volume=749|year=2026|pages=185–196|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2026.06.031|arxiv=2505.22055}}</ref>
